title: Gianna Beretta Molla (1922–1962)
hook: an Italian doctor, wife and mother, honored by the Church as a saint

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Maurin, the wanderer with a plan and a pocket full of short lines. Your line was easy essays. Who heard your idea? Today, a saint with a stethoscope. Day nine hundred fifteen.

A small-town clinic in northern Italy. The doctor on duty is a young woman, seeing mothers, babies and old people, and making house calls when they can't come in. In her free time she skis, climbs, goes to concerts, and paints. She is married to an engineer named Pietro, and they have young children at home. She writes him warm, ordinary letters about meals, trips and the children. Gianna Beretta Molla looks nothing like the saints in old paintings.
screen: `A DOCTOR ON HOUSE CALLS.` → `SKIS, PAINTS, WRITES LETTERS.` → `GIANNA BERETTA MOLLA.`

segments.voice: First, the calling. Gianna trained as a doctor and cared especially for mothers and children. She saw medicine as a way of serving Christ in the sick, and she was active in her parish youth work. Second, the marriage. She thought long about whether to become a missionary or to marry. She married Pietro, and her letters to him are full of joy in plain, everyday things. Third, the choice. During another pregnancy, her doctors found a growth on her womb. There were choices to make. She chose the operation that would remove the growth and protect the pregnancy, knowing it carried more risk for her. Later, she told those around her that if a choice had to be made between her life and the baby's, they should save the baby. Her daughter was born healthy. Gianna died a few days later. Fourth, the saint. The Church has canonized her, and Pietro and their children lived to see it. Catholics honor her choice as a gift freely given, not a rule laid on every mother. Jesus says in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Her letters keep the ordinary days in view as well: a doctor and a mother, at work and at home.
screen: `MEDICINE AS SERVICE.` · `A MARRIAGE OF PLAIN JOYS.` · `SAVE THE BABY.` · `A GIFT, NOT A RULE.` · then, large: `GREATER LOVE THAN THIS NO MAN HATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for mothers who are ill, or hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Let one mother come to mind who is sick right now: your own, a friend, a neighbor, a woman in a hospital you'll never meet. Think of her children, her worries, the doctors and nurses around her. Breathe slowly, as if you were sitting by her bed. If you pray, you can ask Gianna to pray with you for her. If you don't, simply wish her strength and rest. The bell holds the time.
Gianna. The Italian doctor and mother who chose the operation that protected her pregnancy, knowing it carried more risk for her, and whom the Church honors as a saint.
Your line: a doctor and a mother. Today, check on one mother who is unwell, or thank one doctor or nurse who cared for someone you love. Day nine hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Catholics ask St. Gianna Beretta Molla to pray for mothers, families, doctors and the unborn, and some Catholic hospitals and pregnancy centers bear her name.
